newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan cautiously upbeat on future HK business ties.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan cautiously upbeat on future HK business ties.

text.p: Taipei on Tuesday painted an upbeat picture of economic relations with Hong Kong after the freewheeling capitalist territory comes under the control of communist China, Taiwan's bitter adversary.

"We still hold quite an optimistic (view) about, at least, the economic future of Hong Kong," William Li, drafter of a new Taiwan white paper on ties with post-handover Hong Kong, told Reuters Financial Television in an interview.

Li was more cautious on whether Hong Kong's July 1 handover ceremony could do more than break the ice in frosty Taiwan-China relations despite the likelihood that semi-official negotiators from both sides would attend.
"I guess maybe the most they can do is only exchange some opinions on some important issues. That's all," said Li, who oversees Hong Kong and Macau affairs at the cabinet's Mainland Affairs Council.
"For formal negotiations, they have to be authorised by the Mainland Affairs Council," he added.

Koo Chen-fu, head of Taiwan's semi-official Straits Exchange Foundation, has said he would attend the handover. Wang Daohan, his counterpart at Beijing's Association for Relations Across the Taiwan Strait, also was expected at the June 30 gala.
A planned June 1995 Koo-Wang meeting was scrubbed amid new political hostilities and military tensions between Taiwan and China, bitter rivals since a civil war split them in 1949.

Li's 17-page policy paper, issued on Monday by the Mainland Affairs Council, urged Beijing to be practical in handling Taiwan-Hong Kong ties but flatly rejected China's invitation for Taiwan to embrace the "one country, two systems" model of local autonomy that it vows to pioneer in Hong Kong.

Li told Reuters that investment and other Taiwan-Hong Kong business ties should be able to continue and flourish after Hong Kong reverts to Chinese sovereignty on July 1, ending 156 years of British colonial rule.
Hong Kong is the main conduit through which US$30 billion in Taiwan investment has flowed into China since Taipei relaxed a ban on such contacts across the Taiwan strait a decade ago.

Despite increasingly intricate economic ties linking Hong Kong, Taiwan and China, Taipei still bans direct investment in the mainland or official contacts there -- ensuring a crucial middleman role for Hong Kong.
Taiwan executives have expressed concern over Taiwan-Hong Kong relations in the post-handover period, fearing Beijing might use them to squeeze Taipei for political concessions.
Their concerns intensified after Taiwan's ruling Nationalist Party, one of the world's richest, was reported to have moved its Hong Kong holding company to Singapore in February.

Li said such worries were unfounded, citing Hong Kong's well-regarded legal system, a recently enacted Taiwan law to ensure investment confidence July 1 and the sheer weight of current trade and investment ties.
He cited the success of Hong Kong-Taiwan shipping talks in May as an example of "pragmatic" handling of changing ties.
The talks yielded an agreement in which Taiwan and Hong Kong ships would avoid flying flags of the rival sovereigns when entering each other's ports.
